sections.title: Thinking Like a Physicist
sections.learning_target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

i_cans.text: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

ordered_flow.expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students describe variable relationships qualitatively and connect the symbols to physical meaning.

ordered_flow.reference_job: Make explicit that a physics formula is a compact model of a relationship: identify quantities, what is held fixed, and how a change in one affects another.

ordered_flow.purpose: Focus on hypotheses, evidence, law/theory distinctions, and the requirement that scientific claims be testable/falsifiable.

prompt_skeletons: What observation could support this claim?

ordered_flow.expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students name an observable/measurable test and a possible disconfirming result instead of treating plausibility or authority as evidence.

summary_targets: Observation is direct; inference interprets evidence.
Scientific claims must be testable and open to being shown wrong.

sections.title: Forces and Newton’s First Law
sections.learning_target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

i_cans.text: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.
I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.
I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

lets_get_started.job: Skim retained inertia/support-force visuals and headings; notice/wonder about what changes motion and what forces are present.
lets_get_started.focus: Motion can persist with zero net force; multiple real forces may cancel.

i_cans.text: I can explain why force is a vector quantity.
I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.

sections.title: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion
sections.learning_target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

i_cans.text: I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.
I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

sections.source_note: The declared textbook section explicitly states that source content for cp_section_2_7 was unavailable. 4A does not search around that gap; the Framework-required dynamic-equilibrium bridge is mapped from the exact Framework/Bank plus the declared course image toolkit.

vocabulary_preview.job: Terms only; prior-knowledge sort before definitions.

lets_get_started.job: Skim the equilibrium figure(s); notice which forces appear to balance and whether the object must be at rest.
lets_get_started.focus: Equilibrium means ΣF = 0 and unchanged velocity; it can be static or dynamic.

ordered_flow.placement: After Vocabulary Preview and before close reading.
ordered_flow.routing_rule: Use exact canonical Bank WTC content/solution; do not rewrite in 4A.

prompt_skeletons: What forces are actually acting even though the object is at rest?

ordered_flow.expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students distinguish zero net force from zero forces and articulate equal/opposite totals on an axis.

ordered_flow.expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students use force totals, not superficial symmetry, to defend equilibrium.

ordered_flow.reference_job: Distinguish static from dynamic equilibrium: zero net force can describe rest or constant straight-line velocity; equilibrium means no change in velocity, not “not moving.”

prompt_skeletons: Which case is static and which is dynamic?

ordered_flow.expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students use constant velocity—not merely constant speed—as the moving-equilibrium condition and connect it to ΣF = 0.

ordered_flow.routing_rule: Use exact canonical Bank student content and solutions; keep Example immediately paired with its YTI.
Use exact canonical Bank student content and solutions; keep Example immediately paired with its YTI.

summary_targets: Mechanical equilibrium means the vector sum of forces is zero.
Objects at rest can have multiple real forces that balance.
Static equilibrium is rest with zero net force; dynamic equilibrium is constant straight-line velocity with zero net force.
The equilibrium rule can be used separately for up/down and left/right force totals.
